title: Count Words
prompt: Write `count_words(text)` that returns a dict mapping each lowercase word to how many times it appears. Assume words are whitespace-separated.

tests.label: basic
tests.call: count_words('a b a c b a')

hint: Lowercase the text, split on whitespace, then wrap the result in collections.Counter and convert to a plain dict.
explanation: Counter(iterable) tallies items in one call — no manual dict-building loop needed.

title: Most Common Word
prompt: Write `most_common_word(text)` that returns the single most frequent word in `text` (whitespace-separated, no ties in the test cases).

tests.label: basic
tests.call: most_common_word('a b a c a b')

hint: Counter(text.split()).most_common(1) returns a list with one (word, count) tuple — you want the word, the first element of the first tuple.
solution:
from collections import Counter
def most_common_word(text):
    counts = Counter(text.split())
    return counts.most_common(1)[0][0]
explanation: most_common(n) already returns results ranked by frequency, so no manual max-finding logic is needed.

title: Flatten a List of Lists
prompt: Write `flatten_pairs(list_of_lists)` using `itertools.chain` that flattens a list of lists into a single list, preserving order.
hint: itertools.chain.from_iterable(list_of_lists) lazily chains every sublist together; wrap it in list(...) to materialize the result.
explanation: chain.from_iterable avoids a nested loop or list-comprehension-of-comprehensions for the common 'flatten one level' operation.

title: First N Even Numbers
prompt: Write `first_n_evens(numbers, n)` using `itertools.islice` that returns the first `n` even numbers found in `numbers` (an iterable), without processing more of `numbers` than necessary.
hint: Build a generator expression that filters for even numbers, then pass it to itertools.islice(evens, n) and wrap in list(...).
explanation: islice on a generator expression only pulls as many values as needed — it never scans the rest of a huge or infinite iterable once n evens are found.

title: Shopping Cart Total (dataclass)
prompt: Build a dataclass `Item` with fields `name` (str), `price` (float), and `quantity` (int, default `1`), plus a method `total()` returning `price * quantity`. Then write `cart_total(items)` that sums `total()` across a list of `Item` instances.
hint: total() is just self.price * self.quantity. cart_total can use sum(item.total() for item in items) with no explicit loop needed.
explanation: The dataclass gives Item a free __init__ and __repr__; total() is an ordinary method you still write yourself, since dataclasses generate structure, not business logic.

title: Capstone: Inventory Tracker
prompt:
Build an `InventoryTracker` class that combines dataclasses, collections, and functools to track a small inventory.

Implement:
- `__init__(self)` — store an empty `items` list.
- `add_item(self, name, category, price)` — append an `InventoryItem` (a module-level `@dataclass` with fields `name`, `category`, `price`) built from the arguments.
- `total_value(self)` — sum every item's price using `functools.reduce`.
- `group_by_category(self)` — return a dict of `{category: [item names]}` using `collections.defaultdict`.
- `most_common_category(self)` — return the category name appearing most often (using `collections.Counter`), or `None` if there are no items.
- `price_summary(self)` — return `{'min': ..., 'max': ..., 'avg': ...}` across all item prices, or `{'min': None, 'max': None, 'avg': None}` if there are no items.
hint: add_item appends InventoryItem(name, category, price) to self.items. total_value uses functools.reduce(lambda acc, item: acc + item.price, self.items, 0). group_by_category loops over self.items building a defaultdict(list) keyed by category. most_common_category uses Counter(item.category for item in self.items).most_common(1). price_summary computes min/max/avg over [item.price for item in self.items], handling the empty-list case first.
explanation: This mirrors a real internal admin tool: a dataclass models the record shape, defaultdict/Counter aggregate it by category, and reduce composes a running total without a hand-written accumulator loop — the same four stdlib building blocks from this topic's lessons, combined into one class.
